passages.happening:
This is the word of the LORD to Jeremiah about the nations (verse 1), first concerning Egypt and the army of Pharaoh Neco, defeated at Carchemish on the Euphrates by Nebuchadnezzar in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (verse 2).

The poem opens with the army arming: shields ready, horses harnessed, helmets on, spears polished (verses 3 and 4). Then suddenly it is in terror and retreat. The swift cannot flee and the warrior cannot escape; by the Euphrates they stumble and fall (verses 5 and 6). Who is this rising like the Nile? Egypt, boasting that it will rise and cover the earth and destroy cities (verses 7 and 8). Let the chariots charge, with soldiers from Cush, Put and Lud (verse 9).

But that day belongs to the Lord GOD of Hosts, a day of vengeance on his foes (verse 10). The poem pictures the slaughter by the Euphrates as a sacrifice. “Go up to Gilead for balm, O Virgin Daughter of Egypt! In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing” (verse 11). The nations have heard Egypt's shame, as warrior stumbles over warrior (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Carchemish, on the upper Euphrates near today's border of Turkey and Syria, was the site of one of the decisive battles of the ancient world. In 605 BC the Babylonian crown prince Nebuchadnezzar attacked the Egyptian army there under Pharaoh Neco II. The Babylonian Chronicle records the battle as an overwhelming Babylonian victory, with the Egyptian survivors pursued and destroyed near Hamath in Syria. After Carchemish, Babylon, not Egypt, ruled the region.

Egypt rising like the Nile in flood was a fitting boast: the Nile's yearly flood was Egypt's life and pride. The soldiers of Cush, Put and Lud were allies and hired troops from Africa and beyond.

The balm of Gilead returns from chapter 8. Judah had no healing because it would not turn, and Egypt has none either.
passages.later: Zephaniah uses the same picture of judgment as a sacrifice: ‘the LORD has prepared a sacrifice’ (Zephaniah 1:7). Kings records the outcome: Egypt's king ‘did not march out of his land again’ after Babylon took all his territory (2 Kings 24:7).
passages.hard:
Why does the Bible call a bloody battle God's sacrifice and day of vengeance?

Verse 10 pictures the slaughter at Carchemish as a sacrifice held by God, a picture many readers find disturbing. It uses the language of ancient war poetry, and similar pictures appear in Isaiah 34:6 and Zephaniah 1:7. The prophets used such language to say that history's great battles are not random but fall under God's judgment on arrogant powers; Egypt's boast in verse 8, that it would cover the earth and destroy cities, is the pride being judged. Some interpreters stress that this is poetry describing what empires do to each other, read as God's justice, not a celebration of violence. Others stress that the Bible does not shrink from saying God judges nations through war.

The poem concerns Egypt and Babylon as ancient powers in 605 BC. These notes draw no line from it to any nation or state of the present day, and it gives no one a warrant to call any war today God's sacrifice.
passages.asks: Egypt boasted it would cover the earth, and fell in a day. Ask what boast of your own you would not want God to test. And ask what it means that no remedy works for a wound God has not healed.

passages.t: Egypt shamed, and Jacob told not to fear
passages.happening:
The LORD speaks about Nebuchadnezzar coming to strike Egypt (verse 13). It is announced in Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes (verse 14). Why have Egypt's warriors fallen? The LORD drove them down (verse 15). The foreign soldiers say to one another to go home to their own people (verse 16). They call Pharaoh all noise, a king who let his moment pass (verse 17).

One is coming like Tabor among the mountains, like Carmel by the sea (verse 18). Egypt must pack for exile; Memphis will be a ruin (verse 19). ‘Egypt is a beautiful heifer, but a gadfly from the north is coming against her’ (verse 20). Her hired soldiers will turn and run (verse 21). The enemy will come with axes like woodcutters (verse 22). God will punish Amon of Thebes, Pharaoh and Egypt with its gods and kings (verse 25), and hand them to Nebuchadnezzar. ‘But after this, Egypt will be inhabited as in days of old, declares the LORD’ (verse 26).

Then a word to Jacob. ‘But you, O Jacob My servant, do not be afraid’ (verse 27). God will save Israel from far away and bring their children home, and Jacob will have rest (verse 27). ‘For I am with you’ (verse 28). God will not make a full end of Jacob, though he will discipline him justly (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Tabor and Carmel were mountains in the north of Israel that stood out from the land around them. The coming conqueror would stand out the same way.

The beautiful heifer and the gadfly is a homely picture: a fine young cow driven wild by a biting fly. Egypt is great and proud; Babylon is the fly that will send it running.

Amon was the chief god of Thebes, the great city of Upper Egypt. God's judgment falls on Egypt's gods as well as its king.

The oracle does not end with destruction. Egypt will be lived in again, and then, at the end, comes a word for Jacob, repeating 30:10-11: do not be afraid.
passages.later: Isaiah even foresaw Egypt among God's people: “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). Jeremiah had given Jacob the same comfort before (Jeremiah 30:10).
passages.asks: Even in a word against Egypt, God promises that Egypt will be lived in again. Ask whether you can hope for the future of those who have been against you. And ask what fear you need to hear God answer with, do not be afraid.
